reason: The sources provide over 15 consistent claims regarding the tardigrade's discovery, anatomical structure, and unique survival mechanisms, supported by seven independent sites.
story: In 2019, an Israeli spacecraft named Beresheet slammed into the Moon at hundreds of miles per hour. On board were the toughest passengers in the universe: tardigrades. First described in 1773 by Johann Goeze, these "little water bears" look like chubby, eight-legged caterpillars, but they are built differently. When life gets hard, they dry out into a "tun" state, turning their insides into a protective glass using unique proteins. In this state, they have survived all five of Earth’s mass extinctions. They can withstand temperatures near absolute zero, heat past the boiling point of water, and thousands of times more radiation than humans. They even survived 10 days floating in the vacuum of outer space. While they only live a few active weeks, they can stay in their glass-like slumber for decades, just waiting for a drop of water to wake up. They might be microscopic, but they are arguably the most resilient animals on Earth—and possibly now, the Moon.
angle: These microscopic "water bears" can survive the vacuum of space, temperatures near absolute zero, and a high-speed crash into the Moon.

claims.claim: Tardigrades were first described in 1773 by the German zoologist Johann August Ephraim Goeze.
Goeze originally named the creatures "little water bears" (kleiner Wasserbär) due to their bear-like gait.
Lazzaro Spallanzani named the phylum Tardigrada, which means "slow walkers" or "slow steppers."
Tardigrades possess eight legs arranged in four pairs.
They are microscopic animals, typically ranging from 0.05 to 1.2 millimeters in length.
They are commonly known by the nickname "moss piglets."
To survive extreme stress, tardigrades dehydrate and retract their legs into a ball called a "tun."
In the tun state, their metabolism can drop to less than 0.01% of normal levels.
They can survive temperatures as low as −272 °C, nearly absolute zero.
They can withstand extreme heat up to at least 149 °C.
Tardigrades are the only animals known to survive prolonged exposure to the vacuum of outer space.
An Israeli lunar lander named Beresheet crashed on the Moon in 2019 while carrying dehydrated tardigrades.
Water bears have successfully persisted through all five of Earth's mass extinction events.
They produce intrinsically disordered proteins that form a protective glass-like matrix inside their cells.
Tardigrades can survive levels of radiation thousands of times higher than the lethal dose for humans.
They possess two eyespots located in their cerebral ganglion or brain.
Their closest living relatives are arthropods and velvet worms (onychophorans).
Tardigrades can be revived from a dormant state after surviving for over 30 years.
They can endure extreme pressures, including levels up to six times those found in the deepest part of the ocean.
Tardigrades possess a "damage suppressor" (Dsup) protein that protects their DNA from hydroxyl radicals.

disputed: The specific year Lazzaro Spallanzani named the group is cited as 1776 or 1777 (attribute to differing records); the age of the earliest fossils is variously cited as 500 or 600 million years (use 'hundreds of millions'); the maximum survival temperature is reported as 149 or 151 degrees Celsius (state 'approximately 150'); the number of claws per leg was originally described as three by Goeze but modern records state four to eight (attribute to historical versus modern data); and the maximum reported survival time in dry moss varies from 30 to 100 years (state 'decades').
